scenes.title: Cold open
narration: Fire, Myth, and Martial Rhythm: The Ritual Circle of Poorakkali
This is Poorakkali. Traditional.

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Poorakkali originates as a traditional ritual dance performed across North Malabar in Kerala during the nine-day Pooram Thiyya festival.
The practice is anchored in the myth of Kamadeva, who was reduced to ashes by Shiva's third eye when intervening on behalf of Parvati.

Following Vishnu's instructions to the heavenly goddess Rambha to create an image of Kama using flowers and restore worldly joy through song and dance, women on earth initially perpetuated the ritual celebrations.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Poorakkali is enacted exclusively during the nine-day Pooram festival held in the Malayalam month of Meenam (corresponding to the Karthika through Pooram asterisms), honoring the god of love, Kamadeva.
Its ritual foundation recalls the Vasanthapooja performed by dwellers of celestial and earthly realms.
The performance combines sacred education with entertainment, celebrating love's renewal and seasonal revival.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed by an ensemble of young men moving in circular formation around a towering, multi-tiered lit lamp called a nilavilukku.
The dancers execute masculine, acrobatic, and martial art steps characterized by deep physical commitments and agility.
No independent musical players accompany the performance; rhythm is produced entirely by the dancers through synchronized foot-thumping against the ground, hand-clapping, and responsorial singing.
Watch for Synchronised foot-thumping, Panicker call-and-clap.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Poorakkali uses no external instruments, seated percussionists, or separate vocalists.
All musical rhythm and melodic accompaniment are created directly by the performing dancers.
Listen for the Nil (acappella; no musical instruments used; body percussion via clapping and foot-thumping).

A purely acoustic, vocal-and-percussive soundscape stripped of drums or melodic instruments. The Panicker chants episodic verses from classical epics in a ringing voice, immediately mirrored by the deep, unified roar of the male chorus, propelled by loud, sharp clapping and forceful, synchronized floor-strikes.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: The performance takes place within Bhagavathy temple courtyards in North Malabar, centered around a huge, multi-tiered brass lamp (nilavilukku) lit for the occasion.
The dancers are described in sources as young men decked in lion costumes.
Ritual protocols precede the performance, and the dancers undergo a month of rigorous practice alongside strict personal abstinence before stepping into the temple space.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The masters and leaders of Poorakkali are titled Panickers.
They lead the ensemble in song, oversee choreography, direct rehearsals, and are recognized for their historical role in the survival and expansion of the art form.
Marathukali is a distinct, competitive variant of Poorakkali.

Poorakkali reflects generations of artistic transmission among communities in North Malabar such as the Thiyya, Maniyani, and Nambiar, led by lineage masters known as Panickers who preserve the epic hymns, martial choreographies, and temple ritual protocols.
